name: Timestamped track ID questions
insight: The most repeated question across mixes and sets is what a specific track is, almost always pinned to a timestamp. Askers write in English and Spanish, and some just wait for the 'tracklist guy'. Other people answer, so these threads build comment volume on their own.
examples: cual es la cancion del minuto 27:00
use: The track at 0:38 is unreleased. Ask for it and I will tell you when it comes out.

name: Timestamps as praise
insight: When people love a set, they quote the exact minute that hit, so the timestamp becomes the compliment. One commenter notes that a good set shows up as a comment section full of timestamps. A DJ caption that asked people to drop the timestamp matches this habit.
examples: 23:50 was a riot in the back
use: There is one minute in this set where the room changed. Tell me which one you think it was.

name: Brings me back: nostalgia for the original club era
insight: New beat and older wave mixes pull long memory comments. People name their age, the radio station, the club or the sound system, and the decade. Phrases about remembering youth and the 90s repeat many times, mostly from Mexican listeners in Spanish.
use: Built on machines older than some of you. Where were you the first time you heard this kind of beat?

name: Soundtrack to ordinary life
insight: Listeners keep reporting where the music plays: at work, during an assignment, at the gym, at an afterparty, while falling asleep, or early in the morning. Some admit the set distracted them from the work entirely. Asking where people listen gets them to share their routine.
examples: woke up just to watch this
use: Made for late hours in Berlin. Tell me where it ends up playing for you.

name: Let the music run
insight: Fans strongly resent anything that interrupts the flow. A host talking over a set drew a whole cluster of complaints, and others criticised frequent rewinds and clumsy transitions. The shared value is that the music deserves undivided attention.
use: No talking, no reloads. Forty minutes left to run as one piece.

name: New release ritual and the loop
insight: Loyal listeners describe hitting play the moment a new mix drops and listening start to finish. Others put a set on loop because they did not want it to end, or leave comments so a later like reminds them to listen again.
examples: couldn't accept that it had an end
use: New one is out. It is meant to be heard from the first bar to the last.

name: Greetings from / come to my city
insight: Place shows up constantly. People sign off with their country and ask the artist to play their city. Uploaders also ask directly where people are from. This is a reliable comment generator for a touring Berlin artist.
use: Recorded in Berlin. Tell me which city should hear it live next.

name: Feeling words: losing the body, trance, spell
insight: The feeling is described as surrender and being taken over rather than simple happiness. Commenters talk about losing the body to the beat, losing everything but feeling alive, a room put in a trance, mesmerizing or magnetic performances, and a spirit dancing. A dreamlike disbelief shows up too.
examples: lost my body to the beat
use: Somewhere after the second drop the body stops asking permission.

name: Visible joy of the performer
insight: Viewers repeatedly point out that the artist clearly loves what they do. Smiling and enjoying the job is read as part of the set's energy, and some say seeing it live is the only way to understand it. For dark music this is a useful counterweight: warmth behind the shadow is noticed.
examples: putting a smile on so many faces
enjoying what she does for a living
use: Dark music, played with a grin. This is the part of the night I live for.

name: Genre labels and their policing
insight: Titles stack many genre tags, such as dark wave, minimal wave, cold wave and EBM. Commenters push back when the label does not fit, saying tracks are not really new beat or that a set is live rather than DJ. Clear naming of what a track is, and is not, gets noticed and debated.
examples: most of the tracks are not new beat
a live set, not a DJ set
use: Not quite EBM, not quite coldwave. I call it dark dance wave. You can argue in the comments.
